message.content: Lions (family Felidae, order Carnivora) and zebras (family Equidae, order Perissodactyla) diverged from a common ancestor that was an early placental mammal. That ancestor lived roughly 100 million years ago and belonged to the clade Laurasiatheria, the group that gave rise to many modern land mammals.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. This is a biology question. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga). Both are mammals, specifically within the order Carnivora for lion and order Perissodactyla for zebra. But they share a more distant common ancestor at the level of class Mammalia. The common ancestor would be a mammal ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species. That would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae (lion) and Equidae (zebra). That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both families. That might be the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes all placental mammals. So the answer: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammalian ancestor that lived around 100 million years ago, likely a small, insectivorous mammal. But we can give a general answer: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammal that lived about 100 million years ago, belonging to the group of early placental mammals. Or we could say: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a member of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the answer: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria that lived around 100 million years ago.
